issues.legal_issue: A person in settled possession of property cannot be forcibly dispossessed by its owner without recourse to law, even if the person's right to remain in possession is disputed or has allegedly expired.
material_facts: The plaintiff entered possession of the restaurant business and its premises lawfully under an agreement permitting her to conduct the business.

The owner obtained possession behind the plaintiff's back, through collusion with others, and without establishing that the plaintiff had consented or that possession was recovered through legal process.
The trial court and High Court found that the plaintiff had been unlawfully dispossessed and decreed restoration of possession.
The owner argued that the agreement period had expired, but the Court found it unnecessary to decide whether the agreement created a licence or a sub-lease.
issues.conclusion: The owner was not entitled to dispossess the plaintiff unlawfully, and the decree restoring possession was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A person in settled possession may not be forcibly dispossessed, even by the true owner, and the owner must obtain possession through a court. The Court relied on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh, which approved the statement in Midnapur Zamindary Company Limited v. Naresh Narayan Roy that possession in India must be obtained through a court, and on Ram Rattan v. State of Uttar Pradesh. The Court held that the principle applied even though the authorities discussed suits under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 or analogous earlier provisions, because this suit was brought within six months of the dispossession.

predicates.settled_possession_restoration_case: The proceeding seeks restoration of possession after a person has been dispossessed.
predicates.settled_possession: The claimant had established possession of the property before the disputed dispossession.
predicates.owner_used_self_help: The owner took possession without the claimant's consent and without using legal process.

issues.definition: When a restoration proceeding concerns a claimant who was in settled possession and the owner used self-help to dispossess them, the owner must obtain possession through law.

issues.legal_issue: The Court may decline to interfere in a special-leave appeal where the appellant's conduct includes unlawful dispossession and attempts to retain possession through improper means.
material_facts: The appellant had unlawfully taken possession through collusion and behind the plaintiff's back.
The appellant made repeated efforts to retain possession and delay compliance with the possession decree, including bringing a separate suit to obstruct its execution.
The courts below disbelieved the appellant's evidence, and counsel had also recklessly represented that the respondent was dead without first establishing the truth.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under its discretionary appellate jurisdiction, dismissed the appeal, and held that the provisions for special leave were not intended to assist a party with this conduct.
issues.legal_principle: The jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and is not intended to assist a party whose conduct includes unlawful dispossession and efforts to retain possession by improper means. The Court relied on its assessment of the appellant's conduct and cited no earlier case for this point.

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking discretionary special-leave review.
predicates.collusive_self_help_dispossession: The appellant obtained possession through collusion and without the prior possessor's knowledge or consent.
predicates.abusive_obstruction: The appellant used improper or delaying steps to resist compliance with the possession decree.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, collusive self-help dispossession together with abusive obstruction may result in the Court declining appellate interference.

issues.legal_issue: A receiver may be appointed to secure delivery of possession under an affirmed decree when there is a justified apprehension that the decree will be evaded.
material_facts: The respondent expressed a justified apprehension that the appellant would evade the possession decree by putting an outsider in possession or using other underhand means.
The Court had affirmed the decree for possession and appointed the High Court Receiver to take possession from whoever held it and put the respondent in possession as the Receiver's agent.
The Court made the arrangement temporary and subject to further orders by the executing court.
issues.conclusion: The Court appointed the High Court Receiver to take possession of the business and premises from whoever was in possession and to place the respondent in possession as the Receiver's agent.
issues.legal_principle: To secure effective implementation of the possession decree in light of the apprehended evasion, the Court made a protective arrangement through appointment of a receiver; it cited no specific provision or earlier case for this direction.

predicates.enforcement_of_possession_decree: The proceeding concerns enforcement of a decree requiring delivery of possession.
predicates.credible_risk_of_evasion: The circumstances support an apprehension that the person resisting the decree will evade its execution or place another person in possession.

issues.definition: When a possession decree is being enforced and there is a credible risk of evasion, a receiver may be appointed to secure possession.
